content.title: FOOD TRIVIA THAT SOUNDS TOO WEIRD TO BE {{TRUE}}
facts: **Pineapple** is literally digesting you back — it contains bromelain, an enzyme so strong it breaks down protein, which is why your tongue stings after too much.
**Cashew apples** aside, real cashews grow hanging OUTSIDE the fruit, dangling off the bottom like a seed on a stalk — not inside, like every other nut.
**Chewing raw rhubarb leaves** can genuinely poison you — they contain enough oxalic acid to cause organ damage, yet the stalks right next to them are perfectly fine to eat.
**Nutmeg**, in large enough doses, is a legit hallucinogen — just 2 whole nutmegs can cause vivid hallucinations and days-long sickness.
**Wasabi** sold at most restaurants isn't real wasabi at all — it's dyed horseradish, because real wasabi root spoils within minutes of being grated.
**Honey** found in 3,000-year-old Egyptian tombs was still edible — its low moisture and natural acidity make it one of the only foods that essentially never spoils.
**Chili peppers** trick your brain into thinking you're on fire — capsaicin binds to the same receptors that sense actual heat, which is why your body sweats to cool down.
**Avocados** are technically a single-seeded berry, while strawberries and bananas — things that feel far more 'berry-like' — don't botanically qualify as berries at all.

content.caption:
The pineapple fact still gets people — bromelain doesn't just sit there, it actively breaks down the proteins in your tongue and cheeks, which is why pineapple-heavy snacking can leave your mouth feeling raw for a bit. Nutmeg is wild for a different reason: in tiny cooking amounts it's totally harmless, but the same compound (myristicin) that gives it flavor becomes toxic to the nervous system in large doses, which is exactly why it's been used historically as an accidental poison. And wasabi is a fun one because real wasabi root starts losing its pungent compounds within 15 minutes of grating — restaurants simply can't keep up with that shelf life, so dyed horseradish became the industry standard almost everywhere.
